conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go to the ER immediately. Same for severe abdominal pain, confusion, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’re being discharged now in stable condition. Keep taking sucralfate until the 14 days are up, and don’t miss your follow-up endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll mark it on my calendar. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your husband is here to take you home. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid gluten completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. It can cause inflammation and discomfort, even if it’s not the cause of the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be more careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Stay hydrated, rest, and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You came in after your endoscopy and colonoscopy today because you mentioned right upper quadrant pain. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m feeling okay. The pain was bothering me earlier, mostly on the right side under my ribs, but it’s better now. I wasn’t running a fever or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, that’s reassuring. We checked your labs, and your liver enzymes were a bit elevated—AST and ALT were higher than usual, and your bilirubin was up too. Given your history of PSC and past cholangitis, we wanted to keep you overnight to make sure this isn’t turning into an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. So you’re worried about another bout of cholangitis? But I don’t feel sick—no fever, no chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You don’t have the typical signs, which is good. That’s why we’re not starting antibiotics yet. We’re watching closely. If your labs improve and the pain stays gone, we can be confident it’s not active cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. What about the endoscopy? Did they see anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they saw some small to medium varices in your esophagus—some old banding scars and one medium-sized varix with red markings, which means it’s at higher risk for bleeding. They placed one new band on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So that’s why I’m on Carafate again? I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Carafate helps protect the lining and supports healing after banding. You’ll take it four times a day for two weeks. We also continued your omeprazole to reduce stomach acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the colonoscopy? Everything okay there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colon looked mostly normal, but they did notice slightly reduced blood flow in the lining. They took random biopsies to check for any early changes. Nothing urgent, but important for your long-term monitoring given your PSC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, because of the colon cancer risk. I’ll need another one in a few years, I guess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your gastroenterologist will schedule your next surveillance colonoscopy based on those results. For now, we’re focused on your liver and the varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I just reviewed your morning labs. Your bilirubin has already dropped from 2.6 to 1.6, and your AST and ALT are coming down too. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news! So the pain and the liver numbers were just a flare-up, not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks that way. Your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria grew after 48 hours—which supports that. We think this was likely a temporary worsening of your PSC with cholestasis, not bacterial cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried I’d need IV antibiotics again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. You’re tolerating a regular diet, your vitals are stable, and your exam is benign—no tenderness in the abdomen. All signs point to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other meds? I’m on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept everything consistent. You’re still on ursodiol and cholestyramine for your liver, spironolactone and furosemide for fluid balance, rifaximin and lactulose for encephalopathy prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my thyroid and mood meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, levothyroxine for your hypothyroidism, escitalopram daily, and temazepam as needed for sleep. All unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Any pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None at all. I’ve been walking a bit in the hall and feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your liver function is continuing to improve. We’re on track to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about the varices coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common in cirrhosis. That’s why we band them preventively. You’ll need a repeat EGD in six weeks to check healing and see if more bands are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the transplant list? Am I still active?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still listed. Your team is monitoring your status closely. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Final labs look good. Your bilirubin is down to 1.6, transaminases are trending down, and you’ve had no symptoms. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications as prescribed. Finish the full two weeks of Carafate. Stay on your low-sodium diet and fluid restriction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And watch for any warning signs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call your doctor if you develop fever, worsening abdominal pain, jaundice, vomiting, or black stools. Those could signal infection or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a repeat EGD scheduled in six weeks. Your transplant clinic will also be in touch. The biopsy results from the colonoscopy will be sent to your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. A prescription for Carafate has been sent to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing everything’s under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep up with your care plan, and we’ll keep monitoring you. You’re being discharged home in stable condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Continue meds, watch for symptoms, follow up in six weeks. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having this sharp pain in my upper belly, mostly on the right side, and it went into my back. It started suddenly and lasted all night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you have any fever, nausea, or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I felt nauseous and couldn’t keep food down. I checked my temperature and it was 100.2. No vomiting, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of liver disease and past gallbladder surgery, we’re concerned about a few things—like a stone passing or infection. We’ve started some fluids and gave you medication for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time it was something with my liver enzymes. Is it the same thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are actually better than last time. We did check a lipase, which was slightly elevated at 90, but not high enough to suggest pancreatitis. We’re ruling that out with a CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. And the pain? It’s better now, but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good it’s improving. The CT and ultrasound both show your liver is stable, but there are still some stones in your bile ducts. It’s possible one moved and caused the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could they remove it? I don’t want this happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed that. Since your symptoms are improving and labs are stable, the risks of a procedure like ERCP outweigh the benefits right now. We’ll watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the oxygen? I noticed I was on a little at some point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. You were briefly on 2 liters because your oxygen dropped a bit. We think it might have been from the morphine you got in the ER. Your chest X-ray was clear, and you’re now at 97% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s a relief. I was worried about pneumonia or something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection in your lungs. We also drew blood cultures because you had a low fever. One came back with a common skin bacteria—coagulase-negative staph.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It grew in only one bottle, and you’ve stayed fever-free since. It’s likely a contaminant from the blood draw. We started vancomycin just in case, but we’ll stop it tomorrow if no other cultures grow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So no real infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re not showing signs of cholangitis—no high fever, jaundice, or very high liver enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver disease? Is it getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your cirrhosis is still Child-Pugh class B. Your imaging shows stable cirrhosis, splenomegaly, and varices, but no new issues. We’ll keep you on your usual meds—ursodiol, spironolactone, and furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still need the sucralfate? I thought that was just after the last procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing it for now to protect your stomach lining, especially since you’re on several medications. You’ll finish the course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures showed no growth, and your latest labs are stable. We’re stopping vancomycin since the positive culture was likely a contaminant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Much better—you’re only using Tylenol, and your abdomen is only mildly tender. You’re tolerating food well, which is a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried if it comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you get severe pain again, especially with fever or jaundice, you should come in. We might then consider an ERCP to look for stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant status? Is everything on track?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still listed. We sent a hypercoagulability workup in preparation, and those results will go to your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my EGD? Wasn’t I supposed to have a follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your last EGD showed small varices, and one was banded. You’re due for a repeat in six weeks—we’ll make sure that’s scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. Your condition has improved, and we don’t see a need for further intervention right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop worsening pain, fever over 100.3, chills, or yellowing of the skin, please come back right away. Otherwise, keep taking your medications as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood work you sent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The hypercoagulability panel is pending. Your transplant team will follow up on that. No action needed from you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well—vitals stable, pain controlled. We’ll discharge you in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep an eye on your symptoms, take your meds, and follow up with your liver team. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in with fevers and abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I started feeling off two days ago—nauseous and really tired. Then yesterday I spiked a fever and had chills so bad I was shaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the pain—is it in your upper right side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right under my ribs. It’s not as bad now, but it was really sharp earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of primary sclerosing cholangitis, we’re concerned this could be another episode of cholangitis—bile duct inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s happened before. It usually starts just like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs and ultrasound. Your liver enzymes are elevated—especially the alkaline phosphatase—and your bilirubin is up a bit. But no duct dilation on ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no stones blocking anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, but you do have some retained stones in the gallbladder remnant, which we’ve seen before. They’re not causing a blockage now, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the fever? Is it infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think so. We’ve started you on meropenem, a strong IV antibiotic. It’s the one that’s helped you in past episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh good. That usually works for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also watching your kidney function. Your creatinine is a little high—0.9, compared to your usual 0.6. We think it’s from not eating or drinking much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had much appetite. But it’s not my kidneys, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of real kidney disease. We’re giving you IV fluids to help. It should come back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I wanted to let you know your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria grew.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. In cholangitis, cultures don’t always catch the bacteria. Since you’ve responded to meropenem in the past, we’re continuing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I do feel a bit better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But we have another issue—your stool test came back positive for C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: C. diff? From the antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Meropenem can disrupt your gut bacteria. We’re starting you on oral vancomycin four times a day to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay longer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your symptoms. The vancomycin will continue after discharge until your transplant team advises otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Liver enzymes are coming down—ALT and AST are nearly normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. And my creatinine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to 0.5—perfect. Your kidneys have recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m feeling stronger too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to place a PICC line tomorrow so you can finish antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A PICC line? What’s that for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a long-term IV line in your arm. It’ll let you get IV antibiotics at home without daily needles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very. It’s done under ultrasound and X-ray guidance. A specialist will place it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully in your right arm. It’s in the large vein near your heart and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel it. Is it going to be uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people get used to it quickly. A nurse will teach you how to care for it before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep getting antibiotics through it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re switching from meropenem to ertapenem—one dose a day. Easier for home use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: For how long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fourteen days total. Since you started IV antibiotics two days ago, you’ll finish in about 12 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the C. diff medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep taking the vancomycin until your transplant doctors say to stop. It’s important to prevent relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. No fever for two days, labs are much better. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What about my diuretics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting furosemide and spironolactone, but at lower doses—once daily instead of twice. We’ll adjust if you start retaining fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch my weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, check it daily. If you gain more than two pounds in a day, call your liver doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need blood work in two weeks—liver tests, electrolytes, and a complete blood count. Send the results to Dr. Patel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you get fevers, chills, belly pain, or bad diarrhea, come back to the hospital right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right track. Keep following up with your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually approved for a living donor transplant now. That’s a big relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. We’ve coordinated your treatment with that in mind—both the antibiotics and C. diff therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. It feels good to have a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. A nurse will go over your medications and PICC care before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we noticed a small amount of blood in your urine. It’s likely minor, but please repeat a urine test as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even know. I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And don’t forget the lung nodule from your last CT—we’ll need a follow-up scan in a few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll schedule it. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re all rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The home health team will contact you about your IV antibiotics. They’ll help with supplies and training.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be ready for their call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. We’ll see you in follow-up, but call sooner if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.text: Is it getting worse?

conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. When can I go home?
