conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRCP yesterday—special MRI for the liver and bile ducts. It’s completely normal. No blockages, no cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. It means your transplant is working well. The only thing we see is that same soft tissue area, unchanged. We’ll keep an eye on it at your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more IV meds? I’ll just take my regular pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your tacrolimus, CellCept, prednisone—all stay the same. We’re sending you home with tramadol twice a day and extra Zofran if you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Should I be worried about this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to say. Given your history, you might have flare-ups. But now we know infection isn’t likely. Next time, if you’re stable, we may avoid antibiotics unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. I don’t want to be on strong antibiotics if I don’t need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. Your liver team will follow up soon. Keep taking your meds, stay hydrated, and monitor your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. Your vitals are stable, no fever, and your pain is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re sending you with tramadol for pain and Zofran for nausea. Continue all your regular medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel off again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your liver team. If you spike a fever or the pain gets severe, don’t wait—go to the ER. Otherwise, we’ll see you in clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I’m glad we figured out it’s not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Your body’s been through a lot—sometimes symptoms like this are just part of the healing process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It helps to understand it’s not something dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep monitoring, but for now—rest, take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid certain foods with the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to your celiac diet—gluten-free. Otherwise, eat what feels comfortable. Small, frequent meals might help if you feel bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood pressure and sugar—are they okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both are stable. You’re off insulin now, and your BP is well-controlled on lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been walking more since I lost weight—maybe that’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. That’s great for your heart, liver, and overall health. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more question—what about the pleural effusion? The report mentioned it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and unchanged. Probably related to your past surgeries. We’re not worried unless you have shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t. Just glad to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. All in all, you’re in good shape. Discharge papers are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just wanted to say—I’m grateful. You all listened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re here for. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will help you with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had a fever off and on for about a month now. Also headaches, nausea, and muscle aches. No vomiting or diarrhea. My liver doctor told me to come in for evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any neck stiffness, cough, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no neck pain or breathing issues. Just a runny nose sometimes. And I still have that dry cough from my lisinopril—it hasn’t changed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’ve reviewed your labs from the ER. Your white blood cell count is low—2.0—and your neutrophil count is particularly low. That’s called neutropenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that serious? I’ve had low counts before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially since you’re on immunosuppressants. We’re concerned it might be from your medications—like MMF—or possibly a viral infection like CMV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember my last clinic visit—they said my CMV was positive. Should we be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking that. The initial test showed a low level, but the repeat test came back undetectable. So it might have been a false positive. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why the fever and pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have a clear answer yet. Your abdominal pain—mostly in the right lower quadrant—could be related to scar tissue or changes from your transplant. But we’ll keep investigating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an ultrasound of your liver transplant this morning. The blood vessels—portal vein, hepatic artery—are all open and working well. No signs of blockage or fluid collections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. It means your transplant is stable. But it doesn’t explain the fever or low white count. We’re going to adjust your medications to help your counts recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes are we making?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping dapsone—it can suppress bone marrow. We’re switching you to atovaquone, which is safer for your counts. We’re also pausing MMF for now and increasing your prednisone to 10 mg daily to help with immune balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since we don’t have an infection source and your cultures are negative, we’re not starting antibiotics. We’ll keep monitoring your temperature.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count dropped further overnight—ANC down to 440. We’re starting a medication called Neupogen to help your bone marrow make more white cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a shot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a daily injection under the skin. It’s commonly used when counts are very low. It should help your numbers improve over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel bone aches, but we can give acetaminophen if that happens. Most tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your white count is starting to rise. It’s now 3.1. Neupogen is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not quite yet. We still need to figure out the abdominal pain. Given your history, we’re concerned about possible colitis. We’d like to do a colonoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. Is it safe with my low counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s low risk. We’ll do it carefully. We’ll also take biopsies to check for CMV or inflammation in the colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. You did well with the colonoscopy. The colon looked completely normal—no ulcers, no inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We didn’t see anything abnormal, but we took biopsies. Those will take a few days. We’re mainly checking for CMV in the tissue, even though your blood test is negative now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prep—was it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Honestly, it wasn’t the best. We couldn’t fully evaluate for polyps. Since you’ve had adenomas before, you’ll need a repeat screening colonoscopy as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes were stable for most of the stay, but they’ve started to rise a bit. We think it’s because we paused MMF. We’d like to restart it at 500 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But won’t that lower my white count again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Your counts are improving, and we’ve stopped valcyte, which may have been contributing to the suppression. We think it’s safe to restart now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look much better. White count is 4.2, neutrophils are up, and your CMV viral load is still undetectable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the Neupogen worked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and stopping dapsone and valcyte helped too. We’ll stop Neupogen now since your counts are recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about the abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still unclear. The colonoscopy was normal, imaging is fine, and no infection found. We think it may be related to post-surgical changes or nerve irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy results came back. No CMV or inflammation in the colon. So it’s not colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is causing the pain and fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have a definitive answer. The fever has resolved, and your pain is mild. Given all the negative tests, we think it’s likely related to medication effects and your complex transplant history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just one of those things?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Essentially. We’ve addressed the low white count, ruled out serious infections, and your transplant is stable. That’s a win.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re doing well—eating, walking, no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual: tacrolimus, MMF 500 mg twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily. We’ve switched dapsone to atovaquone. And you’ll keep tramadol for pain if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the colonoscopy—do I need another one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as an outpatient. The prep wasn’t adequate, so we couldn’t screen properly. Your liver doctor will schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we’re sending you home with a lidocaine patch for the abdominal discomfort. Apply one patch every 12 hours if the pain bothers you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help with nerve-related pain. It’s safe and doesn’t interact with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: You’ll be discharged tomorrow morning. We’ll arrange outpatient physical therapy for general weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit weak. Is that from the low counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Also from the chronic illness and being in the hospital. PT will help build your strength back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll see my liver doctor soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll review everything, including the biopsy results and schedule your next colonoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just remember: take atovaquone daily, watch for fever or worsening pain, and keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the neurology doctors. You came in with dizziness and a headache—can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I went to bed last night feeling fine, but when I sat up this morning, the room started spinning. I felt like I was on a boat. I had to hold onto furniture to get to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really unsettling. Did the spinning get better when you moved around?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little. The spinning lessened, but I still felt off balance. And then I got a headache—started in the back of my head, now it’s up front. It’s achy and constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea with it? Sensitivity to light or sound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been nauseous. And light and sound bother me a bit. I’ve also been hearing whispers at night—like someone’s talking, but no one’s there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Any weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. My arms and legs feel strong. I do have some word-finding trouble sometimes, but that’s been going on since my transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’re going to do a CT scan of your head to rule out anything serious like a bleed or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m here? Because of a possible stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s one possibility, but your symptoms could also be from inner ear issues or even a medication side effect. The scan will help us rule things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan came back normal—no bleeding or stroke. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But what’s causing the dizziness then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Because your dizziness started after a medication change, we’re considering that as a possible cause. You recently started atovaquone, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about three weeks ago. I was on dapsone before, but they switched me because my white count dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Atovaquone can cause dizziness in some patients. We’re going to order an MRI to get a more detailed look at your brain and blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that tell us for sure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’ll help. If the MRI is normal, it makes a medication side effect more likely. We’ll also check your tacrolimus level—it can sometimes cause headaches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRI results are back. No stroke, no bleeding, no blockages in your brain vessels. Everything looks structurally normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no stroke? That’s great. But what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pattern of your dizziness—worse with movement, better with stillness, and the unsteadiness—suggests a vestibular issue. Given that it started around the time you began atovaquone, we think the medication is likely contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had dizziness before. This feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the timing lines up with starting atovaquone. We’ve discussed this with your liver team, and we agree it’s safe to switch you back to dapsone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my white count dropped last time. Could that happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, which is why we’ll monitor your blood work closely. You’ll need a CBC in one week to check your white count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you ondansetron for that—it should help. We also consulted physical therapy, and they recommend vestibular rehab after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Vestibular rehab? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a type of physical therapy that helps your brain adapt to balance changes. It can reduce dizziness over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to try that. And my headache—is it from the dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your tacrolimus level was high when you arrived—9.2—but it’s come down to 5.5 today. That may have contributed to the headache, but it’s likely also related to the dizziness and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we’re not increasing the dose back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your current dose is appropriate. We’ll keep monitoring it at your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any improvement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little. The nausea is better with the medication. The dizziness is still there, but not as intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Since you’re stable and improving, we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start dapsone instead of atovaquone. Make sure to get your blood work done in one week to check your white count. Also, schedule vestibular therapy and keep your neurology and hepatology follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And if the dizziness gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. If it’s severe or you develop new symptoms like weakness or confusion, come back to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to discharge you this morning. Your dizziness has improved, and all tests are reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with dapsone, continue your other meds, and follow up as planned. Take it slow with activity, and use a cane if you feel unsteady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad we figured it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Me too. We’ll keep working together to manage your symptoms. Safe going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve had this bloating and gas for about a week now. I’m belching a lot and passing gas more than usual. It’s uncomfortable, especially after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just nausea sometimes, no vomiting. I haven’t had fevers, chills, or diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history with the liver transplant and past abdominal issues, we want to make sure nothing serious is going on. We’ll run some blood tests and get an ultrasound of your liver and blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Is this related to my transplant meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. Some immunosuppressants like CellCept can irritate the stomach. We’ll check your tacrolimus levels too—they were a bit high last time, which can cause side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on the same dose. Should we adjust it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see what the labs show. For now, we’ll keep your meds as they are until we have more info.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work came back. Your white count is normal, and your liver enzymes are slightly elevated but stable compared to past results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not alarming, but we’ll keep an eye on it. Your CMV viral load was undetectable, which is great—no sign of infection. Blood and urine cultures also came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the ultrasound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Doppler ultrasound showed your liver blood vessels are open and flowing normally. No blockages or clots. Your liver itself looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a liver issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Doesn’t look like it. The gas and bloating seem more related to your stomach or intestines. We’re considering an upper endoscopy to check for irritation or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel anything. It’s a quick procedure to look inside your stomach and take small tissue samples if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m okay with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule it for tomorrow morning. In the meantime, we’ll start you on simethicone for the gas symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps break up gas bubbles in your stomach and intestines. It’s over-the-counter and very safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I’ll try anything to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Ready for your endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a little nervous but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be asleep the whole time. We’ll update you when you wake up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back in your room. The endoscopy went well. Everything looked normal—no ulcers, no inflammation. We took a few biopsies from your stomach lining just to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. No signs of infection like CMV, and no damage from acid or meds. The biopsies will check for subtle changes, but I’m not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could my celiac disease be acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your tTG IgA level—it was very low, so no sign of gluten exposure or active celiac disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So what’s causing the gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have a clear cause yet. It might be related to your immunosuppressants. We’re going to switch you from Mycophenolate Mofetil to Mycophenolate Sodium—it’s easier on the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe after transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s commonly used. Same active ingredient, just a different formulation. We’ll also lower your tacrolimus dose because your levels were high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: From 2 mg and 1.5 mg to what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll change it to 1.5 mg twice a day. We’ll monitor your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs this morning look stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. But what about the gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve treated what we can in the hospital. The simethicone should help. Since the endoscopy and labs were normal, we’ll refer you to GI for further outpatient workup—maybe dietary causes or bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the biopsies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those results will come in a few days. Your primary team will follow up with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So I stop the old CellCept and start the new one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stop Mycophenolate Mofetil, start Mycophenolate Sodium 360 mg twice a day. Keep taking your tacrolimus 1.5 mg twice daily, pantoprazole, lisinopril, and the others as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And simethicone as needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, up to four times a day for gas. Watch for any new symptoms—fever, severe pain, vomiting—and call your hepatologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon. You’re doing well—just keep up with your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll see my transplant doctor next week. I’m glad we caught the tacrolimus level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was important. High levels can cause side effects, so we’re adjusting it to keep you safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll get you home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in last night with right-sided abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started suddenly the day before yesterday. It’s a dull ache in the upper right side, and it radiates a bit to my back. It’s constant, not worse with eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no vomiting or diarrhea. I’ve just been eating less because of the pain. I did feel chills at home and had a low fever once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your labs and imaging. Your liver enzymes are elevated—ALT and AST are higher than normal. That’s a sign your liver might be irritated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my transplant? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your CT and ultrasound show the liver blood vessels are open and no blockages. But we can’t rule out rejection without a biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A biopsy? Is that safe with my history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll do a transjugular biopsy—through the neck vein. It’s safer for you given your anatomy and blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I trust you. When will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. We’ll keep an eye on your pain and repeat your labs today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we just got back from your biopsy. It went well—you tolerated it fine. They took three samples.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any pain afterward? I feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. There’s a small bandage on your neck. We’ll watch for any bleeding, but it’s very unlikely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will we know the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pathology will take a few days. We’re concerned it could be mild rejection, so we’re adjusting your meds just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your mycophenolate and cyclosporine. And we’re starting prednisone—60 mg daily—to calm any inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Prednisone? I’ve had mood swings with it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that closely. We’re also starting valganciclovir to prevent viral infections, which can mimic rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy results are back. They show mild acute rejection—your immune system is slightly attacking the liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and treatable. We’ve already started the right meds. But your liver enzymes are still rising, which is concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking for infections—CMV, EBV, HSV—but so far, all negative. We may need another biopsy if things don’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling really anxious and restless. I even had some dark thoughts—nothing serious, but it’s not like me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely the steroids. Prednisone can cause mood changes. We’re adding Ativan as needed and starting Seroquel at night to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Seroquel? I’ve heard that can affect the liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, but we’ll monitor closely. Your mental health is important, and this combo usually works well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mood seems better. But your liver enzymes are still going up. We’re switching from oral prednisone to IV solumedrol—stronger dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More steroids? Won’t that make my mood worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we need to control the liver issue. We’re keeping Seroquel and Ativan to help. We’re also holding lisinopril for now—could be contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given 3 grams of solumedrol. But your LFTs are still high. We think it might not be rejection anymore. We’re scheduling a second biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another one? So soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to see if the rejection has responded. We also want to check for drug toxicity or fatty liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Biopsy results are in. Good news—no signs of rejection this time. But there’s mild fatty change in the liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not rejecting? What caused the enzyme rise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s medication-related. Seroquel and temazepam are more likely to cause liver enzyme changes, especially together. We’ll stop both at discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need something for sleep. Temazepam helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you to lorazepam as needed—it’s safer for your liver. And we’ll keep the Ativan for anxiety if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue 20 mg daily for now. Your body needs time to adjust after the rejection scare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And cyclosporine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your level was 262—high, so we’re reducing the dose to 175 mg twice daily. We’ll check it again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been checking my blood sugar. It’s high. Is that the steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, steroids can raise blood sugar. We’re giving you a sliding scale insulin to use at home. It should improve when the dose is lowered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad we figured this out. I was so worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is better, labs are stabilizing. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, blood work in three days—liver tests, cyclosporine level, and basic labs. They’ll be faxed to your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue prednisone 20 mg daily, cyclosporine 175 mg twice daily, mycophenolate 720 mg twice daily, and valganciclovir daily for three months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more Seroquel or temazepam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Use lorazepam for sleep if needed. And the insulin sliding scale—check your blood sugar four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see the liver doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In one week. They’ll review your labs and adjust meds if needed. If your pain returns or you run a fever, call them right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You handled this really well. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I only took Tylenol once yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. And mood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stable. I’m a bit tired, but not anxious like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember, if anything changes, don’t hesitate to call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your husband bring the car around. Take it easy, and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your discharge papers are ready. Lab order is included. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’ve reviewed the discharge instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll get the labs done and follow up next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And remember—no Seroquel or temazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Lorazepam only if I need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing—should I restart my Plavix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart clopidogrel tomorrow. You were off it before the biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I almost forgot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No problem. That’s why we’re here. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final goodbye. You’re officially discharged. We’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team tonight. You came in with fever and right upper belly pain—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up yesterday morning with chills and a fever of 102. I had a headache and body aches all over. Then later, I started feeling pain in my upper right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea, vomiting, or changes in urine or stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. I do have a cough, but it’s been there for a while—my doctor says it’s from my blood pressure medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve run some blood tests and found your liver enzymes are elevated. That’s why we’re concerned. We’re also checking for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this another rejection episode? I had one earlier this year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s one possibility, but we’re also looking at infection or a bile duct issue. Your transplant history makes both concerns important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What tests are you doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already done an ultrasound of your liver and a chest X-ray. The ultrasound shows your liver blood vessels are open and no blockage in the bile ducts. Chest is clear too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the fever and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. We’ve started antibiotics just in case it’s an infection. We’ll keep monitoring your labs and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another biopsy like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hoping not. If your symptoms improve and your liver tests come down, we may avoid it. We’ll reassess in the next day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative so far, and your fever has gone down. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The pain is almost gone, and I don’t feel achy anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your liver enzymes are already starting to improve too. This suggests it wasn’t a serious infection or rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what was it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One possibility is a small gallstone briefly blocked your bile duct and then passed. That could explain the sudden symptoms and quick recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Even though I had my gallbladder out years ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stones can still form in the bile ducts. Since you’re improving, we don’t think further intervention is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Are you still giving me antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop them later today since there’s no sign of infection. You’ll continue your regular transplant meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure medicine? I noticed it wasn’t given last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your lisinopril temporarily in case of infection, but we’ll restart it today since you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look good. Liver enzymes are dropping, and your white blood count is stable. We’re confident you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch you one more night to be safe. If all stays well, you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Should I be worried about this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to predict, but we’ll monitor your liver tests closely. Your transplant team will want to see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs this morning are even better. Liver tests are nearly back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does this mean I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you this afternoon. You’ll need to follow up with your liver doctor and get blood work done early next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What labs do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, and cyclosporine level. You have standing orders at your local lab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling bad again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have fever, chills, belly pain, or jaundice. Also, weigh yourself daily and call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to your usual low-salt, gluten-free diet. Stay hydrated but avoid excess fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, and we’re confident you’re recovering well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it wasn’t something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Keep taking all your medications as prescribed and keep those follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the neurology team. I understand you came in because of facial drooping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I noticed it last night when I was brushing my teeth. The left side of my mouth just felt... loose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you have any other symptoms—like weakness, trouble speaking, or vision changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I could talk fine, no numbness or weakness in my arms or legs. But this morning, it was worse. And my voice sounded kind of nasally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you’ve had a cold and sinus symptoms for about two weeks. Were you on any medication for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was on doxycycline for 10 days, but I stopped a week ago. My cough and sinus pressure are better, but not completely gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Given the sudden onset of facial droop, we need to rule out a stroke. We’ve ordered a CT angiogram of your head and neck to check for any blockages or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A stroke? But I didn’t have any weakness or confusion. Are you sure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important to be cautious. Facial droop can be a sign of a transient ischemic attack—sometimes called a mini-stroke—even without other symptoms. The scan will help us know for sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. Good news—there’s no sign of a stroke, bleed, or major blockage in the brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. So what’s causing the droop then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan did show signs of sinus inflammation—mucosal thickening in your maxillary and ethmoid sinuses. That, combined with your recent infection, makes us think this could be Bell’s palsy, which is facial nerve inflammation often triggered by a viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bell’s palsy? I’ve heard of that. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s usually not dangerous. Most people recover fully over weeks to months. We’ll start you on a steroid to reduce the inflammation and help speed recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just got your MRI results. It confirms no stroke or brain lesion. The sinus inflammation is still there, but nothing else abnormal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely Bell’s palsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your symptoms, normal imaging, and recent illness, yes, that’s the most likely diagnosis. We’ll keep monitoring you, but you’re responding as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. Since your symptoms started recently and there’s no stroke, we’re comfortable discharging you today with oral steroids and instructions to follow up with neurology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I be worried about my liver or transplant history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your transplant team was consulted. They agree your current issue isn’t related to your liver. Just continue your usual medications, including the antiplatelet for your heart health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the breast finding on the scan? Should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There was a small calcified structure noted. It’s not urgent, but we recommend you follow up with your primary doctor for a mammogram to check it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll do that. And if the face doesn’t get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people improve within three weeks. If not, or if you develop new symptoms, contact neurology right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better knowing it’s not a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Rest up, take your meds, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
